utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So, in those two times, that was the only experience you had up until the time you left on August 10th in dealing with any check-points or observations of any check-point; correct?

utterances.speaker: MURRAY DOUGLAS DAWES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. Kehoe [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What's in a name, isn't it? Mr. Dawes, this concludes your evidence. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague for answering the questions that you were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution is prepared to proceed with its next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to raise another matter very briefly, if you would allow me, and then I will give you an opportunity to proceed. There were questions about the bomblets, and it was included in one of the questions that you would need, at least that was suggested, that you would need special equipment to fire them. Now, one of the questions, as I think Mr. Kehoe explained earlier, that it is the first time we hear about these bomblets, but, nevertheless, I wondered whether it's a matter of ammunition that can be fired by normal equipment. We know that, for example, that if you use a mortar, you can load it with all different kind of ammunition, with all different kinds of trigging mechanisms for explosions. Now, one of the things I asked myself is whether firing these bomblets, whether that is a matter of ammunition or whether it's a matter of specific firing equipment which you need to fire that. I'm asking myself whether, although it seems not to be one of the main and big issues in this case, whether the parties have knowledge about it, and whether they could agree on it. That was of no use I think to ask the witness because I did not have the impression that he could help us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can answer the question, Judge, and when he said he didn't know anything further, of course I didn't pursue it. The weapon system that is used for that is called an Orkan rocket system. What it does is it is just like a rocket system that send out multi-barrels. It then goes at a certain altitude, it opens up, and these bomblets come down on the ground. At this particular time, the HV didn't have that. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's not what I asked because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... type of system --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... to evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's not the type of system you that you can put in a mortar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do then understand, if you would agree, Mr. Russo, that this is it a special type of rocket you could fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: - with a multi-barrel rocket launcher. Is that it? If the parties could agree on it or seek agreement on it, so that we know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will say I do not agree with Mr. Kehoe's indication that only the Orkan can do it; however, we can certainly get together and agree about what weapons which were available at the time were cable of either doing that or being modified to do that, as occurred, of course, in the Martic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because reference was made to firing on Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, I'd like to fully understand what we're talking about. If the parties could come any closer to each other in this respect, I would appreciate to be informed about any stipulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Of course, that Martic case was -- that was the one [indiscernible] knowledge on the Orkan rocket system was on the Martic case back in 1995. But we will get together and go through the weapon system available for that such -- that item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Mr. Russo, I interrupted you earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Before moving on, I just want to put on the record that P983 and P984 have both been replaced by the digitally-enhanced images.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw that already for P984 that it has been replaced, when I checked the P984 and 985 issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I was going to ask the Chamber whether we could take an earlier break to switch seats and set up, or if the Prosecution could be given a couple of minutes to do that, whatever the Court's pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to your next witness, Mr. Russo, there are a few outstanding issues, that is, admission in full or in part of the 92 ter statement, that's one; and the second is about an attachment to the 92 ter statement. The Chamber will have to decide on that. Of course, we have looked already at the submissions made in this respect. And before we continue, I would have one question, and I'm specifically addressing the Defence. Is it right that the Prosecution has filed its submission of the 92 ter statement, the motion seeking the 92 ter statement to be admitted on the 23rd of September; and that one of the responses that was the Markac response which was not, at that time at least, opposing the motion in any way, was filed before the 8th of October, but that all other responses were not filed any earlier than the 8th of October, and that is a matter which might be relative under Rule 126 bis which allows two weeks for responses to motions. I'm just checking with we agree on facts. I notice that the Markac Defence, at a later stage, not objecting and joining the Gotovina Defence was also filed after 7th of October. Mr. Kehoe, I'm just trying to verify whether our understand of the facts in this respect are correct and of course if there would be -- if would you like to make any oral submission as far as whether the responses were filed in a timely way then of course we would take one or two minutes for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not sure of the actual dates I know there has been many shifting of witnesses back and forth so if there is any slippage of a day or so in our response certainly it is not prejudicial to the Prosecution on this score in any fashion. So on that level, we would ask the Trial Chamber to accept any of the submissions to the Chamber as submitted. Now, I will say that we have taken another step in this regard as of yesterday. Initially we objected to this summary report that Mr. Hayden is attempting to put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I called the attachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, and given Your Honours' comments yesterday concerning specifically the areas of cross-examination challenging what the witness possibly didn't see in that, and I just note in here that in my motion of yesterday, Your Honour noted at transcript page 10474 -- excuse me, 10,480 at line 25 to 481 at line 1 and 2: "This Court is more interested in what each particular witness has observed outside of the influence of other evidence that other witnesses have provided at least in the first instances." Now, given that guidance ever yesterday one only need to look at two items, again the attachment but also the two statements given by Mr. Hayden. And virtually all of that as can you see by the attachment where we have excluded -- I wouldn't say all of it, quite a bit of that, is simply a rehashing of what over people have told Mr. Hayden. Now, we have a very interesting point on that score. And I only need address Mr. Hayden's recitation of Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes. We have Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes, the author of the provisional assessment and the final assessment on the shelling, who the Prosecution initially had on their witness list, who was taken off the witness list and now through Mr. Hayden is attempting to introduce testimony or comments by Colonel Hjertnes through Mr. Hayden without calling the Colonel Hjertnes. Now given the fact that the Court wants to hear what this witness observed and not what he heard from other people or the rehashing from other people, virtually all of the attachment and a large part of both of his statements are simply that. Simply a rehashing in a different form of what other witnesses have told Mr. Hayden. And if Your Honour's guidance of yesterday has any bearing on this, it clear precludes the entry into evidence of the vast majority of what Mr. Hayden wrote in his statements and I take it his testimony as well. I mean, absent that, Judge, then I will be putting to Mr. Hayden everything that he doesn't know. His categorical statements about the evacuation, statement -- do you know about this, do you know about this, do you know about this before rendering an opinion that the evacuation order was of no consequence? That's where we're going with this cross because that is the only way we're going to be able to meet what he has in these statements which is fine but it is certainly counter to what Your Honour talking to me about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether my comments are put in the right context is still to be seen. The Chamber will consider the matters you have raised. We'll have -- Mr. Tieger before I say that we have an early break you're own your feet, you're even in the courtroom, which I had not noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's like the return of the Maji, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Pleased to be here, Your Honour, and I won't exploit my presence as a basis for making unnecessary comments. It seemed like the Court wanted to consider the context of yesterday's events in terms of the representations made today, and the motion I'll leave it to the Court. If there are any additional questions I will be happy to address them after the break. I did have some comments in response to what Mr. Kehoe said but perhaps it is best if the Court reflects and determine whether or not any observations from the Prosecution are necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it not be better to hear it now, so that we can use the break to consider the matter and we have recent filings on the matter; and therefore, rather than to wait until after the break and then to have to further deliberate on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all as the Court observed we have very recent filings on the matter, which are significantly different from what was filed earlier. In addition, the Prosecution's recollection of the procedural history of the original objections is -- conforms with that of the Court. It is not correct to suggest that yesterday marked some sea change in the approach to matters before this Court or some additional guidance by the Chamber which was not known at the sometime these submissions were originally made. First of all what has been what Mr. Kehoe referred to as the chamber's guidance, I noted were instead a comment by Mr. Russo in respect of the nature of the cross-examination. I think this is an inaccurate attempt to characterize a comment by Mr. Russo about the cross-examination that was taking place yesterday, in which it is very clear from the context that he meant to say what the Court is interested in is what each individual witness has to offer the Court, not in the witness's reaction to the attempt by a party to educate him in court about what he doesn't know. That was the context of the discussion yesterday. And the use of the term "observed" was not meant by Mr. Russo and certainly wasn't guidance by the Court suggesting that the conventional approach to evidential matters before this Court is suddenly being abandoned, and we all know that hearsay is admissible in this institution for various reasons. There was no change in yesterday's proceeding except to the extent that the Court and parties were focussed on the parties between genuine examination in an effort to explore the basis for a witness's opinion or to explore his credibility versus an attempt to use the witness as a platform for argument, and that's all that happened yesterday. Final, with respect to -- to any comments about Mr. Hjertnes it is very clear that Mr. Hjertnes' observations have played a role in this case and have been discussed in this case over and over and over again, to the -- whether or not the Defence will call Mr. Hjertnes or the Court will call Mr. Hjertnes or no one will choose to call Mr. Hjertnes much of his information is before the Court, and it is perfectly appropriate and highly appropriate for the Court hear information that bears on that previous evidence. And finally with respect to an issue that wasn't not addressed although seems to be part of the motion there is, I think, clearly ample and far more than adequate foundation for this report, which was part of the regular procedure prepared in the normal course of business by people who had been exchange in this process before and after and for which the witness was directly involved. This is not a random document that has been produced without understanding of its provenance and foundation. That is all, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Because there are some issues that needed to be address the I think good opportunity for the Court to give us guidance not just for this witness but for the rest of the trial. First with respect to the specific reference to Mr. Hjertnes, I think there is a distinction between the situation where a witness has come up in the course of the trial and a situation where a witness was on the Prosecution's witness list and taken off and then testimony is being introduced, hearsay testimony, of that witness's events. This was a decision made by the Prosecution. The fact that he may be called by the Defence or he may be called by the Bench is irrelevant because as the Court is well aware the Prosecution has the burden of proof. They cannot -- they have to meet their standards and survive a Rule 98 motion at the end of their case in chief, and they shouldn't be allowed to circumvent calling a witness for whatever reason that was done and then to essentially have another witness testify about that witness's testimony that they may think is favourable to believe them. With respect to the more general need, I think, for the parties to obtain some guidance there, there are two issues here. One is in light of what transpired yesterday. The fact is that witnesses as such as Mr. Hayden coming now are providing to a great extent, there are some personal observations, but to a great extent are providing hearsay testimony to the Chamber in any many circumstances hearsay testimony that is not sourced. Either it's our position that that testimony should be excluded or the fact of the matter is the only way that the defendant under Article 21 can challenge such testimony often times is to put other hearsay testimony to that witness in cross-examination which is what happened yesterday, and what ultimately will happen is the Defence is putting matters to a witness that he has no personal knowledge of that flows from the fact that the witness is testifying about matters of which he has no personal knowledge. So we have a situation there where we need guidance from the Court or at least with respect to witnesses that are there providing extensive hearsay testimony some understanding of the position of the Defence that we can't challenge his personal knowledge given that he has very little personal knowledge. The third issue is one that arose today which is this issue again moving toward the future and some guidance from the Chamber. There was an objection by Mr. Russo saying that the witness should -- it's unfair to the witness not to put his statement to him in cross-examination, so he can refer to what he said to the OTP as he is answering questions to the Defence. I rise it my feet because as the Court will recall last Thursday we had a situation where an OTP witness had given a statement to the Defence which in proofing, of course, wasn't shown to that witness as he was being proofed, and we have a statement in evidence that was taken from that witness during the course of his proofing which was taken without the benefit of the OTP showing him the statement that the OTP had in its possession prior to taking the statement. So, from our position, there seems to be some inconsistency in what a witness should or should not be shown. Our position is that we would like some guidance from the Chamber on this process, I think I won't take the Court's time right now; but if we wish to explore it further I think there are some distinctions that need to be made between what the OTP what obligations it has in proofing a witness who is going make attestations under Rule 92 ter and being given the benefit of showing all statements in the possession of the OTP before he is asked to make Rule 92 ter attestations. And also to point out, that in cross-examination I would just ask the Court to keep in mind and all Defence team talked about this during the last break. The fact that a witness on direct can follow what he said in a statement, is of course beneficial to the Prosecution. From the Defence side, we would like to challenge whether he can follow his own testimony without making reference to something on paper, and we think there is beneficial value to being able to see whether the witness on the stand, sitting in the chair has any independent ability to give the Trial Chamber testimony other than what appears on the paper in front of him, so from that perspective we think that there shouldn't be an obligation to necessarily make line and page reference to the witness statement. We all know that the witness can read his own statement; and therefore, our position would that there should be some testing of witness's in cross-examination and indeed that's the very purpose of cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 60 second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. You filed a motion in which you sought admission of 92 ter statement with an attachment. We received your responses, or not but at least responses were filed, let's say it this way. You were given now a multiple responses were filed. Last one yesterday evening. You had an opportunity to respond to that. Now I gave an additional opportunity, I gave it to Mr. Misetic; but I would give it to Mr. Kay and Mr. Kuzmanovic as well. I wonder whether this should not conclude the deliberations on the -- the exchange of views and the submissions on the matter. Because if I give you an opportunity then of course I would have to give an opportunity again to Defence as well. It's -- the initiative was OTP initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay I'm just checking to see the extent to which Mr. Misetic' comments were embraced by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As you'd say if he introduced something knew. That was about guidance but that is matter on which we do not have immediately to decide in every respect. Mr. Misetic, I did not understand your submissions to say well, please give us the guidance right away on all these matters is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I hear the Court, Your Honour. I yield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will have a break and resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber took a bit more time and apologises for any waiting. As far as the 92 ter statements of Mr. Hayden are concerned, the Chamber first would like to verify with - I think it was with you, Mr. Misetic - in relation to the Hjertnes references. We found them in the first statement - let me just find my notes on that - the 1995 statement, we find found them on page 2; and in the 2004 statement, we found them in paragraph 7 and paragraph 26. It was today that specifically Hjertnes was mentioned, and the Chamber considers Hjertnes case as a hearsay source of a bit different character than the general hearsay issues. Have we missed anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I just briefly looked at it, and I believe we're talking about 65 ter 5498 which is the 1996 document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And much of the two documents, Your Honour, are reformulations of each other; and I know in the 2004 document, it is in paragraph 7. There's also a reference to it again on the 2007 [sic] document in paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For 1996, I've got it op page 2; and for the 2004, paragraph 7 and paragraph 26. Did we miss anything, because our attention, of course, was not focussed on that any earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do believe those are the two reports. It is also in several instances in the report itself, the 25 August 1995 Helsinki Report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With specific reference to Mr. Hjertnes as a source?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll further look at that. The Chamber will give the reasons for the decision I now give at a later stage because we want to write it down carefully so that you have all the information which led the Chamber to decide. As far as the 92 ter statements are concerned, the two statements are admitted into evidence, but the specific references to Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes, as we found them until now, on page 2 of the 1996 statement; that is, in paragraph 2 on page 2, starting with the Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes also believed, up to and including, administrative centre of the rebel Republic of Serbian Krajina. Then in the 2004 statement, paragraph 7, in its entirety, is not admitted into evidence. Paragraph 26, the reference to Lieutenant-Colonel Steinar Hjertnes, and we find that approximately in the middle of this paragraph, on page 7: "Further, Lieutenant-Colonel Steinar Hjertnes told us that General Cermak was the military commander for the Knin area," is taken out at well. We will further review, then, the report where specific reference is made to Mr. Hjertnes as the source of the evidence. Apart from that, the 92 ter statements and the attachment are admitted into evidence. I immediately add to that, and that might not come as something new to the parties, that of course to the extent, and we find it here and there, to the extent opinions and conclusions are part of the statement without a proper factual basis be provided, the Chamber, of course, will not be in a position just to adopt it, adopt them as being true. This is not to say that always all the factual basis for an opinion or a judgement should always be found specifically to be given by this same witness. The Chamber looks at the entirety of the evidence, but is not inclined and cannot adopt conclusions just because there were presented by witnesses. The Chamber will always verify whether the factual basis of the evidence allows the Chamber to adopt or join in the conclusions of a witness, because it is not the conclusions of the witness, but it is finally the conclusions of the Chamber that count. Therefore, it may be clear to the Prosecution that where unsourced or undocumented or unsupported opinions or conclusions are presented, that it's certainly worthwhile to see whether there is any factual basis for that. Then, is there any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I just may, for guidance, Your Honour, in the Helsinki Report, 65 ter 796, if we could turn to page 9, and it's 5.4.6. That's 65 ter 769, excuse me. Page 9 of the report is a conversation with Lieutenant-Colonel Steinar Hjertnes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is a specific reference. As I said before, our attention was not focussed on Hjertnes any earlier, but that would be a portion which whether we redact that or whether we say we'll will ignore it, but we have to review the whole of the report on specific references to the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just knew from reviewing it that there had been a reference to it, but I just wanted to bring the Chamber's attention to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Is the ruling clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's clear, Your Honour. I have just one question in connection with that, should Mr. Hjertnes appear in this court. First of all, I obviously can't entirely anticipate the basis for the Court's ruling, but it does occur to me that the rationale might not apply, if he were to appear, and there was an interest in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have added, as a matter of fact, what I had on paper, that at this stage of the proceedings, this is what we want, and that may anticipate what you're asking, that if Mr. Hjertnes comes, then of course either we could ask him whether this is what he said or what he found, or, et cetera; or then to say there's no reason to redact the statements in this respect. The situation be might be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. And then I just wonder about the extent to which that might implicate the interest in cross-examining this witness on that subject, and recalling the witness would be difficult in that context. So I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that point. At the same time, the direct references to Hjertnes are limited. We will consider whether it could be a solution, but then we'd certainly seek also the oral submissions of the parties to, say, deal with it in cross-examination. We'll ignore everything if Hjertnes will not appear, so the cross-examination to be superfluous and without basis, but we have to consider whether that would be a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. I would say, Your Honour, it would sort of the equivalent of the MFI process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I do object to that, Your Honour, given the scenario we have outlined, i.e., if the Prosecution wanted Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes as a witness, he could have testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see. When it comes to that, we'll see, and of course whether you will cross-examine. If I look at one of the portions, for example, that Mr. Hjertnes said what the position of Mr. Cermak was, I don't know whether there's a lot to be cross-examined on that matter, which is apparently now taken out, which is an issue which has been dealt with thoroughly and with many witnesses. So there would be any need at this moment to cross-examine the present witness on that issue, I don't see the point in that, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, let's not, from a theoretical point of view, see what we would do "if." We'll consider it. Cross-examination will certainly not start today, so, therefore, we have some time to think about it. But it's already on the record now that this very cautiously introduced suggestion meets objections from the Prosecution. Then the guidance you asked for, the Chamber will work on that and see to what extent we can give that guidance, but, rather, not do it after having thought it over for five or ten minutes, but, rather, after thorough consideration. Madam Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, perhaps you could also consider to what extent if Mr. Hjertnes would be ever called, whether these issues where his name is specifically mentioned, whether that should be dealt with in the context of this witness's testimony or whether it could be separated and that you just asked Mr. Hjertnes about it, if he would ever appear as a witness, and then Mr. Hjertnes being cross-examined. Whether there is any need to cross cross-examination this witness on hearsay evidence he received from Mr. Hjertnes, but just please think it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will consider it, Your Honour. I was going to respond, but I think it is better done outside the presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hayden. Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing butt truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayden. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, you will first be examined by Mr. Du-Toit who is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: William Curtis Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, can we please call up 65 ter 05498, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, is it correct that on the 15th of May, 1996, you prepared a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, in front of you on the screen, you will see the front page of this statement. Is this the statement that you made and signed at the bottom that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 15th of May, 1996?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also correct that on the 15th of March, 2004, you made another statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can we please call up 65 ter 05499, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, the statement now in front of you on the screen, is that the statement that you made on the 15th of March, 2004?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Can we maybe move to paragraph 5 of the statement. It's on page 2 of the statement, please, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, the last three lines reads as follows: "The facts of this report," and I quote, "are based on rough notes prepared by myself along with other members of the fact-finding mission, named above, during this mission. I do not have the rough notes with me now, but they may be available at home. I will make a search for them on my return and have copies of them transmitted to the OTP when I find them." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Were you able to find copies of these note that the you made subsequently?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: No. The notes were destroyed when my parents' basement flooded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: That happened in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: When did you become aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: After I returned from making the statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, I called my parents, and that's when I learned that the materials that I had stored in their basement had been damaged and/or destroyed by flooding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: If we just move to paragraph 9 of your statement, page 4, please. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: You will see on page 4 about five lines from the top, you make mention, and I quote: "Apart from the UN personnel were confined to various components in the area between 5 and 8 May." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Is May, in fact, the correct date?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: No, it's not, actually. That would be 5 and 8 August. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hayden, is it correct that when you arrived at the Office of the Prosecutor yesterday, you were given again the opportunity to read through the two statements that I just mentioned to you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Except for the amendments that you made and additional information that you provided today, is there anything else that you wanted to inform the Court about that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, do the two statements accurately reflect what you told the Office of the Prosecutor on these two incidents -- on two dates?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And are they, true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And when you -- if you'd been asked to -- the same questions that you have been asked during these interviews, would your answers be the same as you'd given on these two occasions?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to move the two statements into evidence, please, subject to the caveat that the Judge expressed, you know, in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll ask Madam Registrar to assign numbers to them. The decision of the Chamber is clear, but a final admission will be made once the redacted versions will have been uploaded, which the Chamber expects you to do today, Mr. Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, first, the 1996 statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 05498 will become Exhibit P986, Your Honours; and 2004 statement, 65 ter 05499, will become Exhibit P987, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So for the time being, P986 and P987 will marked for identification, and the decision on admission is clear already to the parties on the basis of what I said earlier. Please proceed, Mr. Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, before we move to the report that you prepared, in your two witness statements and also in the report, did you try to inform the reader of information that you personally observed and also information that you received as a result of discussions or other aspects that you had with other witnesses that you mention in your report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may have I on the screen Exhibit -- 65 ter 00769, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, in front of you is now a report, and I quote: "Report to the OSCE, The International Helsinki Federation for Human Rights, Fact-finding Mission to the Krajina, 17-19 August 1995." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And it also appears from the front page of this document that this document was dated the 25th of August, 1995, in Vienna, in Austria. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, can you please in your own words describe to the Court what procedure did you follow in preparing this report that is now in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Typically, a report drafted following a fact-finding mission would be initially based on reports in the media or reports from member committees of the OSCE -- excuse me, member committees of the International Helsinki Federation, regarding human rights abuses that would be of interest. The IHF would then decide to send a fact-finding mission, typically comprised of members of the IHF and members of the national committee of the state in which the human rights abuses were taking place. Once in the field, the mission members would work collaboratively in setting up interviews with persons of interest, conduct those interviews, obtain any documentary evidence or materials that would be of use in preparing the report. The members would work together over their notes, share information, clarify or correct; then the notes would be brought together with any other information, and the report would be drafted, typically by a single person; then the report would be shared with the other members. There would be a review of the document; changes, corrections, or additions made to the report; a final draft would be reviewed by the executive director and legal counsel, before a review by the executive committee, which would then make a decision on its release as a public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned IHF. Can you perhaps tell what you say that stands for?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: The IHF stands for the International Helsinki Federation for Human Rights, a non-governmental organisation based in Vienna, Austria, which functioned as the watch dog of the OSCE, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe; as well as, one could say, the hub of the various national committees that existed in the countries that are members to the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, from your witness statement, it is clear that you were the drafter of this report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, the procedure that you discussed in your evidence so far, was that, in fact, also followed with regard to this report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And the members of the mission that accompanied you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: If we can maybe just move to page 2 of the report, please, and if we go to footnote 1 at the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: The footnote at the bottom identifies the persons that were part of this mission. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, in the report and also in your statement, you sometimes refer to the mission or mission members accompanied or visited this. What do you mean by when you use the word sort of "mission members"? How did you sort of utilize that word in the report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mission members was used as a collective pronoun to describe the individuals noted in footnote 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, if we can go specifically to certain parts of your report, and if I can maybe, firstly, take you to - just a moment - to page 8, paragraph 5.2, and the B/C/S is on page 7. Now, it is clear from paragraph 5.2 of the report that you had a meeting with General Cermak on the 19th of August, 1995, at 1430. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And if we can move to paragraph 5.2.2, it is clear from the report that you also sometimes, not just there but also in other aspects, you use certain words in inverted commas, like done here, stating that: "There are probably 200 to 300 bodies in the hills with bullet wounds in their heads." Now, what procedure did you follow when you put these type of quotations in inverted commas, or what question infer from that when you do that in the report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: The use of commas around text in the report indicates a direct quotation from the person being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Did make a note yourself about that when the person provided you with that information?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes, and the other mission members who were present for that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hayden, you also, subsequent to the meeting that you had with Mr. Cermak on the 19th of August, you also visited the Knin cemetery at around 1530 that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And if we can move to paragraph 4.1 on page 7 of your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Du-Toit, I do not know how much time you are going to spend on what appears to be a new subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Yeah. I think it is an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: An appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, you were only a short time with us today, but we have become desperate, because we would like to see you back tomorrow at 9.00 in this same courtroom. I would first like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given today or still to be given in the following days. We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, the 15th of October, at 9.00, in this same courtroom.
